Connecting again then shows the fingerprint of the new key to confirm.
With StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new, connecting again then takes whatever key the server presents without asking: compare the fingerprint ssh printed above with the administrator first.
With StrictHostKeyChecking yes, connecting again is then refused until the new key is in known_hosts.

With CheckHostIP yes, the address of %1$s may keep the old key on another line, of its own, hashed for instance, or with another name of the same server, and ssh then says it differs from the new one: edit known_hosts in the local shell.
A pattern line for %1$s, which other hosts may match, is left and may hold the old key: edit it in known_hosts in the local shell first, ssh refuses the host until then.

Private keys are encrypted with a key kept in the phone\'s secure hardware, and your fingerprint unlocks them.\n\nShould adding a fingerprint to the phone later destroy them? Someone who learns your PIN then cannot enroll a finger to use your keys, but every stored key is lost, and removing all fingerprints destroys them too.
